screens.title: Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: Open-Source Intelligence, or OSINT, is the practice of collecting measurable and meaningful information from publicly available sources. In this chapter you will learn how to turn widely available web artifacts—search results, social posts, domain records, archived pages, and device banners—into a structured profile of a target. That profile is the starting point for responsible security assessments because it is passive: you are only reading public data, not probing or attacking systems. Practically, you'll learn precise search patterns called Google Dorks, how to read WHOIS and DNS records to map infrastructure, how to mine social media safely for names and roles, and how specialized tools like Maltego and Shodan reveal linkages or exposed devices. As you study these techniques, I want you to focus on three things: accuracy, ethics, and inference. Accuracy means framing queries so results are relevant. Ethics means staying in scope and only using permitted domains. Inference means connecting small facts—an email pattern, a subdomain, a device banner—so they form a useful hypothesis. A quick example: a single exposed PDF mentioning an internal project, combined with a linked LinkedIn post describing that project, can reveal timelines and personnel. Keep that investigative mindset active as we move into concrete operators, commands, and tool examples. How would you check one public clue to see if it links to a larger infrastructure?

screens.title: What is OSINT and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Open-Source Intelligence is the disciplined practice of collecting, validating, and analyzing information that is openly accessible. For an ethical hacker, OSINT provides a legally safe and high-yield starting point because it relies on data intentionally or inadvertently published to the public web: news stories, public databases, social posts, archived pages, and device banners. The key difference between raw public facts and intelligence is context. A single name or an IP address is a fact. Intelligence emerges when you connect facts to support a hypothesis, such as identifying an email format used organization-wide or a forgotten admin page that reveals a legacy service. A concrete example: finding a public PDF on a company site named with an internal project, then confirming via a LinkedIn post that team members worked on that project, gives you a timeline and personnel list. That is intelligence you can responsibly report to the organization. A common misconception is equating OSINT with social media snooping; real OSINT uses diverse sources including WHOIS, DNS, and archived content. As you practice, remember to annotate sources, note dates, and avoid active probing that would cross into scanning. The practical insight is simple: build hypotheses from multiple public clues and validate them before reporting.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › What is OSINT
Definition

OSINT is collecting and analyzing publicly available information. It stays passive and focuses on connecting facts to form useful hypotheses.

Example
A PDF indexed by Google references an internal project. A LinkedIn post from a staff member names the project and date. Together they show scope and personnel.
Common mistake
Treating a single public fact as conclusive without cross-checking other sources.
Key Takeaway

OSINT is passive and evidence-based: collect multiple public signals to form validated intelligence you can report.

Practical checklist
  • Record source URL and capture timestamp.
  • Cross-check names, dates, and file metadata.
  • Note whether data was intentionally published or leaked.
  • Keep activities within authorization and scope.

screens.title: Google Dorking: operators and intent
screens.narratorSegment: Google Dorking is a disciplined way to use search engine operators to limit results and reveal specific file types, pages, or strings. The operators in the chapter—site:, filetype:, intitle:, inurl:, intext:, and cache:—each target a particular field. The process of effective dorking begins with a hypothesis: what artifact are you trying to find? Next, select operators that match that hypothesis. For example, if you suspect confidential PDFs are exposed, you might craft a query that restricts search to the domain, filters for PDF file types, and includes a keyword like confidential. A sample safe practice would be run this on a test domain: site:example. com filetype:pdf confidential. That query narrows millions of pages to documents that match context and format. A common misconception is that more operators always help; in fact, poorly combined operators can return zero results or misleading matches. Start broad, then add operators to refine. Another practical tip: use quotes around multi-word phrases and test different keywords. The process is iterative: form hypothesis, search, review results, refine operators. This disciplined approach increases the signal-to-noise ratio and surfaces files or pages that matter to a security assessment without active scanning.

keyIdea.title: Iterative search process
keyIdea.text: Start with a clear search hypothesis, then apply and refine operators to produce precise, relevant results.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Google Dorking
Dorking process
Form a search hypothesis, select operators that target document type, URL, or title, run the query, then refine based on results. Use quotes for exact phrases.
Common operators
  • site: restrict to a domain
  • filetype: filter by file extension
  • intitle: search page titles
  • inurl: search URL paths
  • intext: search page body text
  • cache: view search engine cached copy
Concrete example
site:example.com filetype:pdf confidential
Run on a safe domain to see how the query filters results to likely sensitive documents.
Pro tip
If a query returns too few results, remove the most restrictive operator and add a keyword instead to widen the net before refining again.
Pitfall
Never perform targeted dorks against live customer domains without written permission; use example.com or explicit test targets.
Try this safely
site:example.com inurl:admin intitle:login
Reflect: what types of pages are surfaced, and why might they be sensitive? Record your answer in the lab report.

screens.title: Concrete dork examples and safe practice
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a few concrete dork examples you should only run on a permitted domain like example. com. Each example illustrates why a specific operator matters. First, site:example. com filetype:pdf confidential targets PDF documents mentioning the keyword confidential. This is useful because internal reports are often stored as PDFs. Second, site:example. com inurl:admin intitle:login looks for URLs containing admin and titles containing login—this helps find forgotten admin panels. Third, site:example. com filetype:xls "passwords" focuses on spreadsheets containing literal password mentions, which represent high-priority findings. As a practical routine, save the query, capture the URL and a screenshot, and note the query time. A common misconception is that a result equals access. Find only what is public; do not attempt to authenticate or exploit. Another tip: try permutations of keywords and file types, and use the search engine cache operator to see previously indexed content. The guided exercise in this chapter asks you to run three safe dorks, record the output, and explain why each result might matter to a defender. That disciplined record keeps your work auditable and defensible.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Dork Examples
Safe example queries
Find PDFs mentioning confidential
site:example.com filetype:pdf confidential
Why: PDFs commonly hold reports and contracts that may reveal sensitive project details.
Locate possible admin login pages
site:example.com inurl:admin intitle:login
Why: Admin panels may be forgotten or misconfigured and reveal management endpoints.
Search spreadsheets for passwords
site:example.com filetype:xls "passwords"
Why: Spreadsheets sometimes store credentials or lists that are high priority to report.
Practice routine
Run queries only on permitted domains, capture URL and timestamp, save screenshots, and write a short rationale for each finding.
Check your understanding
For each dork you run in the lab, record one defender action that would mitigate the exposure revealed by the result.

screens.title: Social media analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Social media platforms surface names, roles, events, and media that often complement other OSINT sources. The goal of social media analysis is not to invade privacy but to collect openly available, public signals that confirm or disprove hypotheses about personnel, technology, or operational practices. For example, LinkedIn can reveal job titles and team structures that help identify key contacts and email formats. Twitter or public posts may reveal event attendance or product names. Images shared on social platforms sometimes show office layouts, equipment, or even documents in the background, which are valid public observations when the content is not behind privacy controls. A concrete practice: identify a public employee profile that lists a role, note the date of the post, and record the publicly displayed handle. Cross-reference that information with other sources rather than assuming accuracy. A common misconception is that all social data is current or accurate; people change roles and may post outdated or personal information. Always note timestamps and validate connections with at least one other public source. In your lab report, include the public URL, a timestamp, and a short explanation of why the information matters for a security assessment.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Social media analysis
What to collect
  • Public names and job titles with profile URLs and timestamps.
  • Images that reveal equipment or layout, noting privacy context.
  • Public posts mentioning projects, events, or vendor names.
Concrete scenario
A LinkedIn job post lists a new cloud migration project. A public Instagram photo from an employee shows a whiteboard with the same project name and a date. Together, these public clues form a timeline and identify responsible teams.
Misconception
Not all social posts are reliable or recent—always capture the date and cross-check with other public records.
Lab task
Find one public staff profile on example.com and record the profile URL, role, and one corroborating public item that links the person to an organizational project.

screens.title: WHOIS and DNS: mapping ownership and infrastructure
screens.narratorSegment: WHOIS databases and DNS records are foundational OSINT sources for mapping a target's ownership and infrastructure. WHOIS queries can show registrant contact names, organizations, registration dates, and name servers. DNS records like A, MX, NS, and TXT map services: A records point to IP addresses, MX records reveal mail servers, NS records show delegated name servers, and TXT records may include service verification or configuration details. Together these records help you understand what systems are associated with a domain and which external providers are involved. A concrete action is to run whois example. com and then dig example. com MX to see mail server hosts. For example, the MX reply might show a host that reveals a third-party mail provider. A common misconception is that WHOIS always reveals personal data; many registrants use privacy services or corporate registration, and GDPR-era records can be redacted. Always interpret the presence or absence of fields cautiously. In a report, include raw WHOIS output and the DNS queries you ran, explain what each record indicates for infrastructure mapping, and note privacy redactions so readers understand limitations.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › WHOIS & DNS
Whois and dig examples
Capture both WHOIS registrations and DNS records to map owner and services. Note redactions and privacy services.
Example commands
whois example.com
dig example.com MX
nslookup -type=TXT example.com
Run these on a lab machine and save the raw outputs for your report.
Record types and meaning
  • A: IP address of a host.
  • MX: mail exchange hosts handling email for the domain.
  • NS: authoritative name servers.
  • TXT: miscellaneous text data, including verification tokens.
Reporting tip
Include raw WHOIS and DNS outputs, annotate key fields, and explain what each record implies about mail or hosting providers and potential attack surfaces.

screens.title: Website analysis: archive.org, robots.txt, and metadata
screens.narratorSegment: Website analysis goes beyond live pages. The Wayback Machine archives historical snapshots that can reveal pages or content removed from the live site. Checking archive. org can surface forgotten directories or earlier versions of pages that expose sensitive information. robots. txt is another simple file that often lists paths site owners prefer crawlers avoid; it does not prevent access but may reveal directories worth checking ethically. Finally, metadata inside images or documents—author fields, software versions, or internal paths—can occasionally provide additional context. A practical example: an archived page from two years ago might show an old admin URL that no longer appears in navigation, or an uploaded document in the archive may contain an author name that ties to a staff profile. A common misconception is treating robots. txt entries as secret; robots. txt is public by design and should only be used as a pointer for further passive research, not as a justification for intrusion. In your analysis, capture archive timestamps, save robots. txt content, and extract metadata from files while noting whether metadata is deliberately published or accidentally embedded. Always annotate provenance so findings are traceable and defensible.

Archive and site files
Check archive snapshots for removed content, examine robots.txt for listed paths, and extract metadata from publicly available files.
Wayback snapshot

screens.title: Maltego vs Shodan
screens.narratorSegment: Two specialized OSINT tools mentioned in this chapter serve different investigative needs. Maltego is a graphical link analysis tool that aggregates data from many public sources and visualizes relationships between entities—emails, domains, names, and social handles—so you can see how facts connect. Shodan, by contrast, indexes banners from internet-connected devices and reveals exposed services, open ports, and device types. Use Maltego when your primary task is to map relationships and build a human-readable graph that supports attribution or social engineering mitigation. Use Shodan when you want to inventory devices that are directly reachable on the internet and to identify misconfigured services. A useful contrast: Maltego helps you trace an email address to domains and social profiles; Shodan helps you find a camera or router that exposes an administrative interface. A common pitfall is confusing data types: Maltego aggregates identity and link data, while Shodan provides host and service-level telemetry. Both tools are powerful and must be used within the engagement scope. In your report, explain which tool you used, what public queries you ran, and why the output mattered to the hypothesis you were testing.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Maltego vs Shodan
Maltego
Graphical link analysis aggregating WHOIS, DNS, social handles, and domain links to visualize relationships and enable attribution hypotheses.
Use-case
Connect an email to a domain and to public social profiles to identify responsible parties or related assets.

screens.narratorSegment: Shodan indexes device banners and service responses, which can reveal software versions, exposed ports, and device types. When you query Shodan, outputs often include an IP address, open ports, the service identified, and a short banner that may state the product or version. This is useful for identifying misconfigured services that are reachable from the internet, such as cameras with default credentials or outdated web servers. A practical pattern is to use a geographic or product filter to prioritize devices and then look for known vulnerable versions. A concrete example is finding an exposed camera interface whose banner reveals the camera model and an HTTP port. This is actionable information for defenders who can then restrict access or update firmware. For ethical practice, perform only passive queries and never attempt to log into discovered devices without explicit permission. Interpreting a banner
A typical Shodan result shows IP, open ports, service name, and banner text that may indicate device type or software version—record all fields and recommend mitigations.
Sample output fields

screens.title: Automating collection: theHarvester and safe aggregation
screens.narratorSegment: Automation tools like theHarvester aggregate data from multiple public sources—search engines, PGP keys, and social platforms—to speed up passive collection. They can collect lists of emails, subdomains, and hostnames that otherwise would take many manual queries. The important skill is to use automation thoughtfully: validate outputs, deduplicate results, and annotate source provenance. Automation increases volume, but not necessarily quality; each aggregated finding still needs a human to verify context and relevance. A concrete workflow: run theHarvester against a permitted domain to produce an initial list of subdomains, then manually verify the most promising entries with a WHOIS query or a targeted search dork. A common mistake is treating every returned item as valid—automated tools can return false positives or entries pulled from outdated caches. In your lab, use automation to create a candidate list, then show two manual verifications for different item types. This pattern—automate broadly, verify selectively—keeps you efficient and produces defensible findings for reporting. Automated collection pattern
Run an aggregator to collect candidate emails, subdomains, and hostnames, then validate the highest-priority results manually and capture source evidence.
Example step
theHarvester -d example.com -b google
Review the output, then validate an email or subdomain with separate queries before recording it as evidence.
Workflow tip

Lab task

screens.title: Ethics, scope, and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Ethics and scope are central to OSINT practice. Passive collection of publicly available information is legal in many jurisdictions, but ethical constraints and engagement rules still apply. Always confirm the target and domain are in-scope and have written permission if a test is part of an engagement. Avoid targeted searches on third-party or customer domains without explicit approval. Common mistakes include confusing public exposure with permission to access, failing to document timestamps and sources, and treating single results as definitive evidence. Each of these errors undermines the defensibility of your findings. A practical reporting habit is to include: the exact search query you ran, the captured URLs or outputs, timestamps, and an explanation of why the finding matters and how a defender could mitigate it. For example, if you discover a publicly indexed spreadsheet containing credentials, include the search terms, the URL, and a recommended mitigation such as removing the file or restricting access. End each finding with an inference confidence level—low, medium, or high—based on how many sources corroborate it. This discipline keeps your OSINT work actionable, auditable, and aligned with ethical testing practices.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Ethics & Mistakes
Ethical checklist
  • Confirm scope and written permission before targeted queries on non-test domains.

Common mistakes
Treating an exposed fact as permission to access, failing to document provenance, and over-relying on a single source are frequent errors that make reports unusable.

Query, captured URL, timestamp, raw output, interpretation, confidence level, and mitigation recommendation.

fullNarratorScript:
Open-Source Intelligence, or OSINT, is the practice of collecting measurable and meaningful information from publicly available sources. In this chapter you will learn how to turn widely available web artifacts—search results, social posts, domain records, archived pages, and device banners—into a structured profile of a target. That profile is the starting point for responsible security assessments because it is passive: you are only reading public data, not probing or attacking systems. Practically, you'll learn precise search patterns called Google Dorks, how to read WHOIS and DNS records to map infrastructure, how to mine social media safely for names and roles, and how specialized tools like Maltego and Shodan reveal linkages or exposed devices. As you study these techniques, I want you to focus on three things: accuracy, ethics, and inference. Accuracy means framing queries so results are relevant. Ethics means staying in scope and only using permitted domains. Inference means connecting small facts—an email pattern, a subdomain, a device banner—so they form a useful hypothesis. A quick example: a single exposed PDF mentioning an internal project, combined with a linked LinkedIn post describing that project, can reveal timelines and personnel. Keep that investigative mindset active as we move into concrete operators, commands, and tool examples. How would you check one public clue to see if it links to a larger infrastructure?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to apply a set of OSINT techniques that are essential during the footprinting phase. First, you will learn to use advanced search engine operators—sometimes called Google Dorking—to narrow results and find exposed documents or forgotten admin pages. An example task is using a combination like site:, filetype:, and inurl: to find PDFs or login pages that may be indexed unintentionally. Second, you will gain practical skills in social media analysis: identifying public employee profiles, job titles, and shared media that may reveal equipment or internal processes. In practice, a LinkedIn search can reveal an email format used across an organization, which is valuable for reporting and safe phishing simulations. These objectives emphasize legality and ethics. You will practice only on a safe domain such as example. com or on explicit test targets. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone that helps you demonstrate skill responsibly. Throughout, reflect on the difference between collecting public clues and performing intrusive scans. That distinction is essential to remain within legal boundaries during any engagement.

This companion objectives slide frames the same learning outcomes as competency checks. We emphasize not only what you can find but how you verify findings and report them responsibly. For Google Dorking, the competency is to craft targeted queries that reduce noise and surface sensitive material on a test domain. For social media, competence means extracting names and roles in a way that supports a hypothesis but does not cross privacy boundaries. For WHOIS and DNS, you will demonstrate the ability to interpret A, MX, NS and TXT records and to explain why each record matters to mapping infrastructure. For tools, you will explain when Maltego's link analysis gives value and when Shodan's device banner index is relevant, and you will note the difference between passive queries and active scanning. Each objective includes a micro-milestone that can be checked in a short lab report: sample dork, captured WHOIS fields, a named social clue with a safe screenshot, and a short justification for choosing Maltego or Shodan in an assessed scenario. These checks ensure you can apply knowledge ethically and explain why a finding is important for defensive teams.

Open-Source Intelligence is the disciplined practice of collecting, validating, and analyzing information that is openly accessible. For an ethical hacker, OSINT provides a legally safe and high-yield starting point because it relies on data intentionally or inadvertently published to the public web: news stories, public databases, social posts, archived pages, and device banners. The key difference between raw public facts and intelligence is context. A single name or an IP address is a fact. Intelligence emerges when you connect facts to support a hypothesis, such as identifying an email format used organization-wide or a forgotten admin page that reveals a legacy service. A concrete example: finding a public PDF on a company site named with an internal project, then confirming via a LinkedIn post that team members worked on that project, gives you a timeline and personnel list. That is intelligence you can responsibly report to the organization. A common misconception is equating OSINT with social media snooping; real OSINT uses diverse sources including WHOIS, DNS, and archived content. As you practice, remember to annotate sources, note dates, and avoid active probing that would cross into scanning. The practical insight is simple: build hypotheses from multiple public clues and validate them before reporting.

Google Dorking is a disciplined way to use search engine operators to limit results and reveal specific file types, pages, or strings. The operators in the chapter—site:, filetype:, intitle:, inurl:, intext:, and cache:—each target a particular field. The process of effective dorking begins with a hypothesis: what artifact are you trying to find? Next, select operators that match that hypothesis. For example, if you suspect confidential PDFs are exposed, you might craft a query that restricts search to the domain, filters for PDF file types, and includes a keyword like confidential. A sample safe practice would be run this on a test domain: site:example. com filetype:pdf confidential. That query narrows millions of pages to documents that match context and format. A common misconception is that more operators always help; in fact, poorly combined operators can return zero results or misleading matches. Start broad, then add operators to refine. Another practical tip: use quotes around multi-word phrases and test different keywords. The process is iterative: form hypothesis, search, review results, refine operators. This disciplined approach increases the signal-to-noise ratio and surfaces files or pages that matter to a security assessment without active scanning.

Let's walk through a few concrete dork examples you should only run on a permitted domain like example. com. Each example illustrates why a specific operator matters. First, site:example. com filetype:pdf confidential targets PDF documents mentioning the keyword confidential. This is useful because internal reports are often stored as PDFs. Second, site:example. com inurl:admin intitle:login looks for URLs containing admin and titles containing login—this helps find forgotten admin panels. Third, site:example. com filetype:xls "passwords" focuses on spreadsheets containing literal password mentions, which represent high-priority findings. As a practical routine, save the query, capture the URL and a screenshot, and note the query time. A common misconception is that a result equals access. Find only what is public; do not attempt to authenticate or exploit. Another tip: try permutations of keywords and file types, and use the search engine cache operator to see previously indexed content. The guided exercise in this chapter asks you to run three safe dorks, record the output, and explain why each result might matter to a defender. That disciplined record keeps your work auditable and defensible.

Social media platforms surface names, roles, events, and media that often complement other OSINT sources. The goal of social media analysis is not to invade privacy but to collect openly available, public signals that confirm or disprove hypotheses about personnel, technology, or operational practices. For example, LinkedIn can reveal job titles and team structures that help identify key contacts and email formats. Twitter or public posts may reveal event attendance or product names. Images shared on social platforms sometimes show office layouts, equipment, or even documents in the background, which are valid public observations when the content is not behind privacy controls. A concrete practice: identify a public employee profile that lists a role, note the date of the post, and record the publicly displayed handle. Cross-reference that information with other sources rather than assuming accuracy. A common misconception is that all social data is current or accurate; people change roles and may post outdated or personal information. Always note timestamps and validate connections with at least one other public source. In your lab report, include the public URL, a timestamp, and a short explanation of why the information matters for a security assessment.

WHOIS databases and DNS records are foundational OSINT sources for mapping a target's ownership and infrastructure. WHOIS queries can show registrant contact names, organizations, registration dates, and name servers. DNS records like A, MX, NS, and TXT map services: A records point to IP addresses, MX records reveal mail servers, NS records show delegated name servers, and TXT records may include service verification or configuration details. Together these records help you understand what systems are associated with a domain and which external providers are involved. A concrete action is to run whois example. com and then dig example. com MX to see mail server hosts. For example, the MX reply might show a host that reveals a third-party mail provider. A common misconception is that WHOIS always reveals personal data; many registrants use privacy services or corporate registration, and GDPR-era records can be redacted. Always interpret the presence or absence of fields cautiously. In a report, include raw WHOIS output and the DNS queries you ran, explain what each record indicates for infrastructure mapping, and note privacy redactions so readers understand limitations.

Website analysis goes beyond live pages. The Wayback Machine archives historical snapshots that can reveal pages or content removed from the live site. Checking archive. org can surface forgotten directories or earlier versions of pages that expose sensitive information. robots. txt is another simple file that often lists paths site owners prefer crawlers avoid; it does not prevent access but may reveal directories worth checking ethically. Finally, metadata inside images or documents—author fields, software versions, or internal paths—can occasionally provide additional context. A practical example: an archived page from two years ago might show an old admin URL that no longer appears in navigation, or an uploaded document in the archive may contain an author name that ties to a staff profile. A common misconception is treating robots. txt entries as secret; robots. txt is public by design and should only be used as a pointer for further passive research, not as a justification for intrusion. In your analysis, capture archive timestamps, save robots. txt content, and extract metadata from files while noting whether metadata is deliberately published or accidentally embedded. Always annotate provenance so findings are traceable and defensible.

Two specialized OSINT tools mentioned in this chapter serve different investigative needs. Maltego is a graphical link analysis tool that aggregates data from many public sources and visualizes relationships between entities—emails, domains, names, and social handles—so you can see how facts connect. Shodan, by contrast, indexes banners from internet-connected devices and reveals exposed services, open ports, and device types.
